name: visitor
intent: Represent an operation to be performed on the elements of an object structure, so that new operations can be defined and added over a stable element hierarchy without changing the classes of the elements on which they operate.
problem: A heterogeneous structure (an AST, a document or widget tree, a shape or entity hierarchy) needs many independent operations, and they keep arriving: every new analysis, export format, validation or report adds another method to every element class, mixes unrelated concerns into the data model and forces the hierarchy to be recompiled. Moving the operation into a separate object does not solve it by itself either, because with single dispatch a call like visitor.visit(element) can only select on the visitor's type, never on the element's concrete class.
context: Applies when the element classes are stable or closed while operations over them are frequent, when the elements must not be edited (third-party, generated or shared model code), when the language offers single dispatch only, and when operations must stay open to other teams or modules. Typical settings: compiler and analyzer passes, document and tree exporters, tree-shaped domain models, and plugin-facing extension points over a class hierarchy.
benefits: Adding an operation requires no change to the element classes: it is one new visitor class (or one dispatch function) in its own module, which keeps the data model closed for modification and open for extension.

Behaviour is localised: one operation over many classes lives in one place instead of being spread across every element class, and the visitor can keep private helper state (accumulators, traversal depth, output buffers) that would otherwise be threaded through the elements.
Concrete element classes are detected by polymorphic dispatch instead of instanceof/type tests, so the operation gets correct per-class handling with no casts and no silent default branch.

Traversal and operation vary independently: the same visitor runs over different walk orders (full tree, filtered walk, streamed subtrees), and the same structure is visited by an unbounded set of operations, including ones written by other teams.

Operations become first-class values: they can be configured, decorated, tested in isolation and selected at run time, which is what makes Visitor a natural extension point for tooling and plugin systems.

Double dispatch enables type-safe operation selection based on both the visitor and element runtime types, providing compile-time safety in languages that support method overloading with specific parameter types.
tradeoffs: Adding a new ConcreteElement is expensive: the Visitor interface gains a method and every existing concrete visitor must implement it — in a published API this is a source-incompatible change (the JDK documents exactly this for javax.lang.model.element.ElementVisitor and recommends abstract adapter classes as the mitigation).

Encapsulation is weakened: visitors can only use what the elements publish, so elements grow accessors (or friend/package-private pacts) that exist solely to feed the operation, enlarging the public surface of the data model.
Every visit costs two virtual dispatches plus the traversal machinery, and the operation is harder to inline than a direct method call; on hot paths over tiny elements this shows up in profiles.

Responsibility for traversal must be assigned: elements recursing inside accept() couple the structure to the walk policy, while clients walking the structure re-implement the walk once per operation — and the two options differ when nodes are added, moved or streamed.
Visitors that hold state (current depth, current file, collected diagnostics) cannot be shared between traversals or threads; the pattern pushes you towards one throwaway instance per walk.

The dependency direction is inverted: the element hierarchy must know the visitor interface, so the assumption that the structure is stable is what justifies the coupling — if elements change as often as operations, the pattern adds cost without benefit.
In languages with native multimethods or exhaustive pattern matching over sealed/enum hierarchies, visitor adds boilerplate for a capability the language already provides more concisely.
The visitor hierarchy must know every concrete element type, creating a hard dependency cycle between the two hierarchies in languages without separate interface compilation.

participants.responsibility: Declares one visit operation per class of ConcreteElement in the object structure; the parameter type (or method name, where the language has no overloading) identifies which element class the operation handles, and a state parameter or return type carries the operation's result.
Implements each visit operation, realizing one complete operation over the structure, and may accumulate state between visits (results, diagnostics, current position).

Declares the accept(Visitor) operation; it is the only hook the element hierarchy has to expose for the pattern, so the element is coupled to the visitor abstraction and not to any concrete operation.
Implements accept by calling back the visitor method for its own concrete class (visitor.visitThis(this)); that callback is the second dispatch and the reason no type test is needed.
Owns or exposes the elements and lets the visitor reach them — a Composite tree that recurses into its children, a collection whose iterator feeds accept, or the element itself for a single node.
Creates the concrete visitor, starts the traversal (usually accept on the root or a loop over the collection) and reads back the accumulated result.

use_cases: Compiler and analyzer passes over an AST: type checking, constant folding, liveness analysis, code generation and pretty-printing are separate visitors over the same node classes.
Serializers and exporters over a document object model: HTML, PDF and Markdown renderers, accessibility audits and word counts all walk the same node hierarchy.

Public analysis APIs that let other people add rules without touching the model — the JDK's javax.lang.model.element.ElementVisitor and Roslyn's CSharpSyntaxVisitor are this pattern shipped as stable API.
Geometry, CAD and UI trees where area, bounding box, hit testing, transform and persistence are independent operations over a fixed shape or widget hierarchy.
Metrics, pricing and validation passes over domain models (billing rules, insurance rating, tax) where new report variants must ship without recompiling the entity classes.
Plugin systems where third parties implement operations over a host's object graph and the host enumerates available operations by their visitor type.

Linter and static-analysis rule engines (ESLint, typescript-eslint, clang-tidy): each rule is a visitor over the ESTree or Clang AST, keyed by node type; traversal is driven by the framework and rules are stateless functions with a context/report parameter.

Refactoring and code-rewrite tools (Roslyn CSharpSyntaxRewriter, OpenRewrite): a specialised visitor subclass returns modified nodes, enabling transformations across the tree in a single pass without mutable state.

Database query engines that build, optimise or execute query plans over typed AST nodes (e.g., JPA Criteria API, Hibernate's static metamodel, Apache Calcite's rel nodes): each physical operator or optimisation rule is a visitor over the plan tree.

Automated code transformation and migration frameworks (jscodeshift, codemod): one visitor per transformation script walks the AST and applies replace/edit operations; the same framework hosts hundreds of community-provided scripts.

Babel AST processing: @babel/types and @babel/traverse expose a Visitor object whose methods are keyed by AST node type (e.g., visitIdentifier, visitFunctionDeclaration); plugins return a Visitor that the traverse pipeline applies, supporting :exit suffixes for post-order traversal and selector strings for compound node matching.

OpenRewrite recipe framework: recipes are stateless visitor subclasses over typed AST nodes (Java, Python, YAML, Docker); the framework handles traversal, scope management and patch application, while recipe authors implement only the visit methods for the node types relevant to their transformation.

Abstract syntax tree traversal in program analysis tools: every time a new analysis is needed (security scan, code quality check, dependency finder), it can be implemented as a new visitor without modifying the AST node classes.
Serialization frameworks (XML/JSON marshalling): each serialization format (XML, JSON, YAML) is a separate visitor that walks the object graph and formats it accordingly.
Document conversion pipelines: converting between formats (Markdown to HTML, DOCX to PDF) where each format is a visitor that knows how to render each document element type.

CPython's ast module ships NodeVisitor in the standard library: subclass it with visit_<TypeName> methods, visit() dispatches on the node class name at runtime, generic_visit() descends into children, and the NodeTransformer subclass rewrites trees by returning replacement nodes — returning None deletes the node.

.NET ships System.Linq.Expressions.ExpressionVisitor in the BCL: Expression.Accept(ExpressionVisitor) is the accept() hook, Visit dispatches to VisitBinary/VisitLambda/VisitMethodCall per expression node type, and every LINQ provider subclasses it to inspect or rewrite query trees before translating them to SQL.

clang libTooling: RecursiveASTVisitor<Derived> (a CRTP template) walks the C++ AST via Traverse*/WalkUpFrom*/Visit* hooks dispatched on the node's dynamic type; clang-tidy checks and clang tools are ASTConsumer plus RecursiveASTVisitor pairs — the canonical C++ realisation, replacing the GoF virtual Visitor interface with templates.
avoid_when: The element set is closed and the language has exhaustive dispatch (sealed hierarchies with pattern matching, enums, discriminated unions): one match/switch function per operation is shorter and the compiler still proves coverage.

Adding element types is the frequent change rather than adding operations — put the behaviour on the elements themselves, or move to the Acyclic Visitor / Extensible Visitor forms so new elements do not touch every visitor.
The operation touches one or two element classes, or there is no traversal at all: a plain method, a function, or a strategy is simpler and keeps the call sites readable.
The structure is unstable or ad hoc (dictionaries, JSON documents, a List<object>): normalise it into a typed hierarchy first, because a visitor over an untyped bag buys no dispatch safety.

You control neither the elements nor a framework-provided visitor (there is no accept to call and the hierarchy cannot be extended): a dispatch table keyed by type, an extension object, or an anti-corruption layer is the practical alternative.

You have many element types and few operations (the classic visitor explosion): each new operation adds a new visitor class; if operations are truly independent, consider the Strategy pattern or a dispatch table instead.
The visitor pattern would require modifying third-party or generated code that cannot be changed: use a dispatch table or wrapper layer instead.
anti_patterns: A visitor that does the type test: one visit(element) with instanceof/type-switch inside, while the elements still expose accept() — both halves of the dispatch and none of the guarantees.
One visitor class that implements every operation (PrintAndCheckAndCountVisitor), reintroducing the god class the pattern exists to split.
Mutating the structure from inside a visit callback (inserting, removing or replacing nodes mid-traversal) without a defined policy.
Making every hierarchy a visitor target 'for extensibility', paying the coupling and the boilerplate everywhere and using it nowhere.
Sharing one stateful visitor instance across traversals or threads to avoid allocations — the accumulated state then leaks between walks.
Cyclic visitor: a visitor that calls back into the element hierarchy from inside a visit method, potentially causing infinite recursion on circular object graphs without a guard.
design_principles: Open/closed principle: operations are open for extension while the element classes stay closed for modification.
Single responsibility: one visitor holds one operation; the element holds data and its invariants.
Separation of concerns and double dispatch: the algorithm lives outside the data structure, and the concrete element class is detected by polymorphism rather than by type tests.
Dependency inversion: elements depend on the Visitor abstraction, not on concrete operations, which is what allows the two hierarchies to be compiled and shipped separately.
Composition over inheritance for behaviour: operations are assembled from visitor objects instead of being piled into element subclasses.

Expression problem resolution: visitor is the classical OOP solution to the expression problem — the ability to add new operations over a fixed type hierarchy without modifying the types — whereas multimethods and pattern matching are the functional counterpart.

Interface segregation: the Visitor interface should be as small as possible; if only some operations need certain element types, consider the Acyclic Visitor to avoid forcing implementations to handle irrelevant types.
best_practices: Keep accept() implementations one-liners (visitor.visitThis(this)); the callback belongs in the element, but no logic does.

Put the traversal in exactly one place: either composite elements recurse into their children from accept(), or a shared traversal helper walks the structure — never let each visitor re-implement the walk.
Ship a no-op base visitor or abstract adapter so a new element type does not break every operation immediately; this is what AbstractElementVisitor in javax.lang.model and DefaultVisit in Roslyn do.

Prefer stateless visitors with an explicit accumulator (a generics parameter, a second parameter, or a returned value) over visitors that mutate themselves, so one instance can safely serve several traversals.
Expose exactly the element accessors the operations need and keep them read-only; if visitors must write, add a separate mutation interface with its own policy instead of widening the read surface.
Register or enumerate operations where the caller can choose them (a registry, a plugin list), so the element module never depends on the operation module.
When the element set is closed and the language can prove exhaustiveness, prefer the language's match/switch form and keep Visitor for hierarchies that stay open or belong to someone else.

Prefer external visitors (client drives traversal) over internal visitors (visitor drives traversal) when the same structure needs multiple walk orders or streamed/lazy traversal, because internal visitors hard-code the walk policy.
Use a visitor argument (ctx, state, accumulator) passed on every visit call rather than mutating visitor fields; this makes the visitor reusable and thread-safe without re-instantiation.
When performance matters on hot paths, consider an inline variant: a sealed hierarchy with a match expression generates a single dispatch table lookup rather than two virtual calls.

For plugin-facing APIs, ship an Abstract*Visitor adapter that provides a default implementation of every visit method (often a no-op or identity pass-through); this keeps third-party plugins compiling even when you add a new element type.

If the element hierarchy is owned by a third party (e.g., a language model's AST from a compiler library), never add accept() yourself — use the framework's provided visitor base class or a dispatch table keyed by type.

When implementing a family of related visitors (e.g., all code-quality rules in a linter), factor the shared traversal into a shared Walker base class and let each rule override only the visit methods it cares about.

In Python, prefer ast.NodeVisitor for AST walking (reflective dispatch, no accept needed) over hand-rolled double dispatch; use functools.singledispatch for simple function-based dispatch and structural pattern matching (Python 3.10+) for closed hierarchies.

In Rust, prefer enum + match for closed hierarchies you own — it is zero-cost, exhaustive and compiler-checked; reserve trait-object visitor only for genuinely open hierarchies extended by third parties.

In TypeScript, use discriminated unions with exhaustive switch/match for closed hierarchies (the never type enforces completeness); reserve the visitor interface + accept form only for plugin-facing APIs where the AST is external.
For Babel plugins: use the visitor object with methods named after AST node types; leverage the :exit suffix for post-order operations and path.skip() to prune subtrees.
For ESLint rules: each rule returns a visitor object from create(context); use context.report() with a messageId for testable errors and a fix function for auto-fixable violations.
Consider the visitor explosion problem: if you have N element types and M operations, you need N×M implementations. If both N and M are large, reconsider whether visitor is the right choice.
sources: Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson & John Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) — Visitor (Behavioral Patterns chapter, pp. 331 ff.): intent, participants, double-dispatch mechanics, consequences (adding ConcreteElement is hard, encapsulation trade-off, traversal responsibility assignment).

Tanumoy Pati & James H. Hill, "A survey report of enhancements to the visitor software design pattern," Software: Practice and Experience 44(6):699–733 (2014) — comprehensive taxonomy of extended Visitor variants (Reflective Visitor, Walkabout, Dynamic Dispatcher) and alternative patterns; classifies enhancements as structure-preserving vs structure-modifying.

Robert J. McCauley, "The essence of the Visitor pattern" (IEEE COMPSAC 1998) — refines GoF Visitor via the Walkabout pattern; eliminates the accept-method requirement using reflection for dynamic class discovery, expanding applicability to late-bound object structures.

Jeremy Gibbons, "The Visitor Pattern as a Reusable, Generic, Type-Safe Component" (Oxford, 2005) — formalises Visitor in terms of catamorphisms and F-algebras; connects the pattern to recursion schemes and generic programming.
Object Mentor, "Visitor Pattern" (air.cpp — Robert C. Martin series) — double-dispatch mechanics, open/closed consequence, traversal policy trade-offs, abstract adapter as mitigation.

Oracle, Java SE 11 API: javax.lang.model.element.ElementVisitor — the JDK's canonical shipped-as-API visitor; documents the AbstractElementVisitor adapter and the design constraint that adding new Element subtypes is a source-incompatible change.

dotnet/roslyn, CSharpSyntaxVisitor.cs — Roslyn's shipped C# compiler API visitor; implements DefaultVisit fallback, Generic CSharpSyntaxVisitor<TResult>, CSharpSyntaxWalker (depth-first traversal), and CSharpSyntaxRewriter (non-mutating traversal with structural rewrite hooks).

ESLint, "Custom Rules" — the ESLint rule API uses a visitor object returned from create(context); keys are ESTree node types with optional :exit suffix for post-order; supports selector strings for compound matching and onCodePathStart/onCodePathEnd hooks.
typescript-eslint, "Custom Rules" — TypeScript-ESLint visitor pattern over the TypeScript ESTree superset; uses @typescript-eslint/rule-tester with messageId-based error assertions.

Stack Overflow, "What is the point of accept() method in Visitor pattern?" — clarifies why accept() is needed for double dispatch and why calling visitor.visit() directly leaks element knowledge to the client.

Stack Overflow, "Why do we start Visitor by calling Acceptor.accept(), and not Visitor.visit()?" — explains how accept(visitor) preserves encapsulation by keeping traversal logic inside the element; visitor.visit() directly would expose element internals.

rs4ts.dev, "The Visitor Pattern" (2024) — contrasts GoF double-dispatch visitor with Rust's enum+match approach; explains when to use trait-object visitor in Rust (open extensibility) vs enum+match (closed hierarchies owned by the crate); connects to the Expression Problem.

Software Patterns Lexicon, "Visitor Pattern in Python" (2023) — covers Python ast.NodeVisitor reflective dispatch, functools.singledispatch for function-based dispatch, and structural pattern matching as modern alternatives; practical guidance on when visitor beats simpler alternatives.

Software Patterns Lexicon, "Visitor Pattern via Double Dispatch in Rust" (2023) — explains how Rust simulates double dispatch via its trait system; contrasts idiomatic enum+match with the GoF trait-object form for open hierarchies.

APIDesign Wiki, "Visitor" — evolvable API guidance: versioned immutable Visitor interfaces per language version, bridging factory to connect clients to evolving providers, and default-method pitfalls for version extension.

Nice (nice.sourceforge.net), "Visitor pattern considered useless" — critique of visitor boilerplate and complexity; demonstrates multimethods as a shorter, more natural solution to the expression problem in languages without single-dispatch constraints.

Castor (wxzh.github.io), "Programming with Extensible Generative Visitors" (SCP 2020) — presents extensible generative visitors as a modular alternative to GoF visitor; addresses accept-method intrusiveness and demonstrates the approach in a research compiler framework.

jOOQ Blog, "The Visitor Pattern Re-visited" (2019) — contrasts visitor with composite for SQL query rendering; shows how jOOQ's DSL avoids the visitor explosion problem for queries with many expression types.

nipafx.dev, "Visitor Pattern Considered Pointless — Use Pattern Switches Instead" (2020) — argues that Java's classic visitor adds more complexity than a plain pattern switch for closed hierarchies; demonstrates how sealed classes + pattern matching (Java 17+) eliminate most visitor use cases in Java.

MartinLwx, "Understanding Visitor Pattern: the art of double dispatch" (2026) — thorough explanation of double dispatch mechanics, how two single dispatches compose to simulate multiple dispatch, and when visitor excels in AST processing contexts.
Refactoring Guru, "Visitor and Double Dispatch" — explains the dispatch binding problem (late vs early, static vs dynamic) and how double dispatch resolves the ambiguity that single dispatch cannot.
Inspirel, "Visitor Revisited" — critical analysis of visitor pattern's violations of OCP, encapsulation trade-offs, and comparison with simple switch-based alternatives in non-OOP languages.

Didier Verna, "Revisiting the Visitor: the 'Just Do It' Pattern" (J. UCS 2010) — demonstrates how visitor becomes unnecessary in dynamic languages with multimethods (CLOS); introduces iceberg metaphor showing patterns as language-specific idioms with submerged support.
Baeldung, "Visitor Design Pattern in Java" — practical Java implementation guide covering double dispatch, open/closed benefits, and pitfalls when adding new element types.

CSSEMediaWiki, "Visitor" — academic analysis of visitor pattern including conflicts with Demeter's Law, encapsulation violations, and cyclic dependency issues; mitigation strategies with Bob Martin's Acyclic Visitor.

BestHub, "Why Mediator, Visitor, and Interpreter Are the Rarest Design Patterns" (2026) — examines narrow applicability of visitor, its hostility to adding new element types, and recommends sealed class + pattern matching as modern replacement in Java.
Hemaks, "Crafting Your Own Babel Plugins" (2025) — practical guide to Babel plugin development using the visitor pattern; covers visitor structure, path manipulation, and testing strategies.

OpenReplay, "Inside the AST: How Tools Understand Code" (2026) — explains how ESLint, Prettier, Babel, and TypeScript use the visitor pattern over Abstract Syntax Trees; contrasts with Concrete Syntax Trees and mentions Rust-based alternatives like Biome.
JS Guide, "Custom ESLint Rules & Plugins" (2025) — comprehensive guide to writing custom ESLint rules using AST visitors, including meta/create structure, context.report(), and auto-fix patterns.

Read OSS, "AST Types, the Visitor Pattern, and Scope Analysis in Babel" (2026) — deep dive into @babel/types and @babel/traverse internals: VISITOR_KEYS registry, alias expansion, enter/exit lifecycle, visitor merging across plugins, and scope tracking mechanism.

Python Software Foundation, "ast — Abstract Syntax Trees" — the stdlib NodeVisitor: runtime name-resolved visit_<TypeName> dispatch, generic_visit() fallback that must be called explicitly to descend into children, NodeTransformer for rewrites where a None return deletes the node; visit_Str/visit_Num deprecated in favour of visit_Constant.

Microsoft Learn, ExpressionVisitor (System.Linq.Expressions) — the .NET BCL visitor over expression trees: Visit dispatches to VisitBinary, VisitBlock, VisitLambda, VisitMethodCall, VisitExtension and friends, returning the possibly-rewritten tree.

Microsoft Learn, Expression.Accept(ExpressionVisitor) — accept() shipped in the base class library: the expression-side entry point of the double-dispatch pair, forwarding to the visitor's type-specific Visit method.

Clang documentation, "How to write RecursiveASTVisitor based ASTFrontendActions" — libTooling guide: subclass RecursiveASTVisitor<T> (CRTP), implement VisitCXXRecordDecl-style hooks returning bool, drive the walk from an ASTConsumer with TraverseDecl; returning false aborts traversal.

Clang API reference, RecursiveASTVisitor<Derived> — three-tier dispatch Traverse*/WalkUpFrom*/Visit* on the node's dynamic type with shouldVisitImplicitCode() and shouldTraversePostOrder() policy hooks; how clang avoids the GoF virtual-interface visitor in C++.

swiftlang/swift-syntax, "SwiftSyntax" official package documentation — SyntaxVisitor traverses the typed syntax tree with per-node-type visit methods and visitPre/visitPost hooks; SyntaxAnyVisitor trades traversal performance for a single visitAny entry point.

swiftlang/swift-syntax, SyntaxRewriter.swift — generated tree-rebuilding rewriter: rewrite(_:) returns a new tree, visitAny(_:) can replace a subtree, visitPre/visitPost bracket the walk and visit(TokenSyntax) enables token-level rewriting.
pitfalls: A visitor that does the type test: one visit(element) with instanceof/type-switch inside, while the elements still expose accept() — both halves of the dispatch and none of the guarantees.
One visitor class that implements every operation (PrintAndCheckAndCountVisitor), reintroducing the god class the pattern exists to split.
Mutating the structure from inside a visit callback (inserting, removing or replacing nodes mid-traversal) without a defined policy.
Making every hierarchy a visitor target 'for extensibility', paying the coupling and the boilerplate everywhere and using it nowhere.
Sharing one stateful visitor instance across traversals or threads to avoid allocations — the accumulated state then leaks between walks.

Skipping the no-op base visitor and growing the Visitor interface without defaults, which breaks every existing operation at once when a new element is added — the JDK's own ElementVisitor documents exactly this source-incompatibility hazard.
Implementing accept() once on the base class with a type test instead of overriding it in each concrete element — the callback then passes the base type and the compiler can no longer check coverage.
Letting every visitor re-implement the traversal: two operations then disagree about visit order and double-visit different nodes.
An internal visitor that hard-codes the walk policy (depth-first, pre-order) makes it impossible to stream a large tree, filter nodes, or switch to breadth-first without rewriting every visitor.
Adding an accept() method to third-party element classes that are generated or version-pinned — instead use the framework's provided visitor base class or a type-keyed dispatch table.
Cyclic visitor: a visitor that calls back into the element hierarchy from inside a visit method, potentially causing infinite recursion on circular object graphs without a guard.
Using the Acyclic Visitor's dynamic_cast to break dependency cycles adds runtime type-check overhead that can become a bottleneck in tight traversal loops over large trees.

Interface bloat: as the element hierarchy grows, the Visitor interface accumulates visit methods, making it large and fragile — each new element type requires updating the interface and every existing implementation.
Violating encapsulation by adding 'visitor-friendly' accessors to element classes solely for the visitor's benefit, exposing internal state that would otherwise be hidden.

Visitor explosion: when both the number of element types AND the number of operations are large (N×M problem), visitor requires implementing N×M combinations; consider whether a simpler pattern or restructuring the hierarchy would reduce complexity.
Over-intrusive accept(): requiring elements to know about the visitor hierarchy violates separation of concerns and can introduce unwanted dependencies in systems where elements should be standalone.
Forgetting to call generic_visit() (or equivalent) in Python ast.NodeVisitor subclasses causes child nodes to be silently skipped, leading to incomplete analysis.
Assuming visitor is needed where a simple Strategy or function would suffice: visitor adds significant boilerplate for cases where only one or two element types are involved.

Wrong move: stash the parent or ancestor chain in a mutable visitor field to give visit methods the context accept() never passes -> failure: an exception unwinding mid-walk or a reused shared instance desynchronises the stack and the visitor silently analyses with the wrong ancestors -> instead: carry context on the path or node (Babel NodePath, Roslyn SyntaxNode.Parent, swift-syntax parent pointers) or pass it explicitly through the recursion.

Wrong move: implement rewrite-style visitors as in-place mutation or without honouring the framework's return contract -> failure: CPython's ast.NodeTransformer silently deletes any node whose visit_<Type> method returns None, and mutating nodes in place corrupts the structural-sharing rebuild Roslyn rewriters and swift-syntax SyntaxRewriter depend on -> instead: return the (possibly rebuilt) node and let the framework reassemble the tree.

Wrong move: depend on runtime name-keyed dispatch conventions to stay correct -> failure: a misspelled or stale visit method is never called and never reported, and taxonomy changes strand them — CPython deprecated visit_Str/visit_Num into visit_Constant leaving old methods dead -> instead: assert per-type coverage in tests or prefer generated typed visit methods (Roslyn, swift-syntax) that fail at compile time.
